questions.q: How do standard CTEs (the WITH clause) behave in Snowflake compared to T-SQL?
options: Identically — no syntax changes are needed
Snowflake does not support the WITH clause at all
Snowflake requires a different keyword entirely for non-recursive CTEs
CTEs can only be used once per query in Snowflake
questions.explain: Standard CTEs, including multiple and chained CTEs, work exactly the same in Snowflake as in T-SQL.

questions.q: Which window functions transfer directly from T-SQL to Snowflake with the same names and OVER() syntax?
options: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), LAG(), and LEAD(), among others
None — Snowflake uses entirely different function names for ranking
Only ROW_NUMBER() transfers; the others require different syntax
Window functions do not exist in Snowflake
questions.explain: Snowflake supports the same ranking and offset window functions as T-SQL, with identical names and PARTITION BY / ORDER BY syntax.

questions.q: What is the key syntax difference for recursive CTEs in Snowflake compared to T-SQL?
options: Snowflake requires the RECURSIVE keyword explicitly (WITH RECURSIVE), while T-SQL infers it
Snowflake does not support recursive CTEs at all
Snowflake requires UNION instead of UNION ALL for the recursive member
Recursive CTEs require a stored procedure in Snowflake
questions.explain: T-SQL infers recursion from the CTE structure, but Snowflake requires you to explicitly write WITH RECURSIVE — omitting it causes a syntax error.

questions.q: What happens if you write a recursive CTE in Snowflake without the RECURSIVE keyword?
options: Snowflake throws a syntax error
It silently runs as a non-recursive query with no error
It automatically adds the keyword for you
It runs correctly with no difference in behavior
questions.explain: Unlike silently misbehaving, Snowflake raises a syntax error when RECURSIVE is missing from a recursive CTE definition.

questions.q: What relationship does QUALIFY have to the classic 'top N per group' CTE + ROW_NUMBER() pattern?
options: QUALIFY produces the same result in one query, without needing a wrapping CTE — both approaches are correct Snowflake SQL
QUALIFY replaces ROW_NUMBER() entirely and cannot be used alongside it
QUALIFY only works with recursive CTEs
QUALIFY is required and the CTE pattern no longer works in Snowflake
questions.explain: QUALIFY is a Snowflake-specific shortcut for the same top-N-per-group logic — the CTE + WHERE rn = 1 pattern still works fine, QUALIFY is just more concise.
